exact_final_saved_claim.justification: The same 36-week assessment point, BPD criteria, and oxygen-reduction approach apply to both randomized groups; trial personnel and outcome assessors were blinded. For eligible infants, oxygen-reduction testing was not performed in similar proportions (13/86 vs 13/94). No group-specific threshold or assessment method is reported. This supports probably no differential measurement; the exact assessment opportunity for every participant is not fully detailed.
unknowns: Outcome information was unavailable for some participants and reasons for all missing oxygen assessments are not fully reported; this relates chiefly to D3 availability rather than showing differential measurement.

4|Randomization
5|Dynamic randomization was performed with a
6|secure Web-based system that was created and
7|hosted by the NPEU Clinical Trials Unit with
8|24/7 telephone backup, ensuring concealment of
9|the group assignments. The randomization pro-
10|gram used a probabilistic minimization algorithm
11|and assigned patients in a 1:1 ratio to one of the
12|two groups to ensure balance with respect to the
13|size of the PDA, gestational age at birth, age, sex,
14|trial site, whether the infant was from a multiple
15|birth, mode of respiratory support, and whether
16|inotropes were received. Infants in multiple births
17|underwent randomization individually. Partici-
18|pants were enrolled by the delegated clinician at
19|the trial site.14
20|Intervention and Trial Procedures
21|The trial intervention was ibuprofen sodium,
22|and the matched placebo was a clear sterile solu-
23|tion of 0.9% sodium chloride. Each carton con-
24|taining ibuprofen or placebo was labeled with a
25|unique code in compliance with the guidance
26|provided in annex 13 of the European Commis-
27|sion guidelines for Good Manufacturing Prac-
28|tice. Ibuprofen was administered parenterally as
29|a loading dose of 10 mg per kilogram of body
30|weight, followed by two doses of 5 mg per kilo-
31|gram at least 24 hours apart. Placebo was ad-
32|ministered as an equal volume of 0.9% sodium
33|chloride (Table S2). Only one course of ibuprofen
34|or placebo was given. Prespecified criteria for
35|open-label medical or surgical treatment after
36|enrollment are shown in Table S3.
37|Transthoracic echocardiography was performed
38|to assess eligibility within 72 hours after birth
39|and at 3 weeks (18 to 24 days) of age to assess the
40|patency of the PDA while minimizing open-label
41|treatment. For quality control, a sample of echo-
42|cardiograms from 65 infants was reviewed inde-
43|pendently by a pediatric echocardiographer who
44|was unaware of the treatment assignments.
45|Outcomes
46|The primary outcome was a composite of death
47|or moderate or severe bronchopulmonary dyspla-
48|sia assessed at 36 weeks of postmenstrual age15
49|(Tables S4 and S5). A physiological challenge of
50|supplemental oxygen reduction was used to test
51|for oxygen need at 36 weeks of postmenstrual
52|age16 to differentiate mild from moderate bron-
53|chopulmonary dysplasia (Fig. S1). Secondary
54|short-term outcomes up to the time of discharge
55|included individual components of the primary
56|outcome, the severity of bronchopulmonary dys-
57|plasia, severe intraventricular hemorrhage, cystic
58|periventricular leukomalacia, retinopathy of pre-
59|maturity requiring treatment, clinically signifi-
60|cant pulmonary hemorrhage, acute pulmonary
61|hypertension, definitive necrotizing enterocoli-
62|tis, closed or clinically nonsignificant PDA less
63|than 1.5 mm in diameter with restricted flow at
64|3 weeks age, open-label treatment of a PDA caus-
65|ing symptoms, weight gain, and discharge home
66|while receiving supplemental oxygen (Table
67|S5).14 Other secondary short-term outcomes are
68|listed in the Supplementary Appendix and in the
69|statistical analysis plan (available with the pro-
70|tocol).17 All outcome data were recorded rou-
71|tinely, including demographic data and compli-
72|cations of prematurity; these data were obtained
73|from clinical notes or trial-related assessments
74|(Table S6).
75|A list of foreseeable serious adverse events
76|that are common in this patient population was
77|prespecified (see section 9.1.4 in the protocol);
78|unforeseeable serious adverse events were de-
79|fined as those that were not included on this
80|list. A serious adverse reaction was defined as a
81|serious adverse event that was considered to
82|have been caused by the administration of the
83|trial agent; if such an event was not consistent
84|with the safety profile of the trial agent, it was
85|classed as a suspected unexpected serious ad-
86|verse reaction.14
87|Statistical Analysis
88|The incidence of the primary outcome was pre-
89|dicted to be 60% in the placebo group (see Sup-
90|plementary Methods). A sample of 730 infants was
91|calculated to be required in order to detect a
92|clinically important absolute risk reduction of 12
93|percentage points (i.e., an incidence of 60% in
94|the placebo group and an incidence of 48% in the
95|ibuprofen group) with 90% power and a type I
96|error of 5% under the assumption that 1% of in-
97|fants would be lost to follow-up.14
98|Analyses were performed according to the
99|intention-to-treat principle, with infants exclud-

exact_final_saved_claim.justification: The SAP specifies the ITT Cox analysis and enumerates primary censoring and sensitivity analyses, including plausible missing-follow-up event imputation; the article reports the primary ITT and per-protocol estimates and says prespecified sensitivity results appear in Figure S9. Although analyses were multiple, the inspected material does not indicate selective reporting based on results.

6|The contribution of each component of the primary composite safety/efficacy endpoint to the
7|overall treatment effect will be examined.
8|Event rates of the primary composite CV endpoint will be estimated and Kaplan-Meier curves
9|will be plotted for the time from randomization to first occurrence of the primary composite
10|CV endpoint, by treatment group and prior CV risk at randomization based on IVRS.
11|Homogeneity of the effect of treatment on the components of the primary safety/efficacy CV
12|composite endpoint will be assessed using the method proposed by Lunn and McNeil9 (1995).
13|Briefly, this method requires augmenting the analysis dataset by including one observation per
14|component of the CV composite per subject, with an additional variable indicating the type of
15|the potential event (CV-related death, nonfatal MI, nonfatal stroke). If a patient experienced
16|an event which counted as the first instance of the CV composite endpoint, the event status
17|for that event will be one and it will be zero for the other two types of events, which will be
18|censored at the time the first event occurred. If a patient did not have CV composite endpoint,
19|event status will be zero for all three component types of events. For example, if a patient had
20|nonfatal MI on day 270 which counted as his first occurrence of the CV composite, he would
21|have three observations in the analysis dataset: 1) type=nonfatal MI, status=1, time=270; 2)
22|type=nonfatal stroke, status=0, time=270; 3) type=CV death, status=0, time=270. The
23|augmented dataset will be analyzed using Cox regression with (time, status) as response
24|variables and event type, treatment and treatment by event type interaction as covariates. To
25|account for the use of multiple observations per subject in the analysis, Lin-Wei robust
26|sandwich variance3 will be used. The test of treatment by event type interaction will be the test
27|of homogeneity of treatment effect on the components of the CV composite endpoint. Hazard
28|ratios and 95% CIs for treatment effect on each component of the primary endpoint will be
29|produced.
30|4.5.1.1
31|Primary Safety Analysis: Non-inferiority of EQW versus Placebo
32|To determine whether EQW is non-inferior to placebo, a non-inferiority margin of 1.30 in
33|terms of hazard ratio with respect to developing the primary composite CV endpoint will be
34|used.
35|The primary safety hypothesis (H1) is defined as:
36|H0: HR ≥ 1.3 vs. H1: HR < 1.3
37|The hypothesis of non-inferiority will be tested at a one-sided significance level of 0.02495 in
38|the ITT population using a Cox Proportional Hazards model which includes treatment as
39|explanatory factor with prior CV event at randomization based on IVRS as a stratification
40|factor. The two-sided 95% confidence interval for the hazard ratio of EQW to placebo will be
41|estimated. If the upper limit of the two-sided confidence interval for the estimated HR for the
42|stratified Cox model is below the non-inferiority margin of 1.30 then non-inferiority of the

25|secondary efficacy endpoints (null hypothesis is denoted as H0[51], H0[52],) will be tested
26|at one-sided 0.02495 level by using the same Hochberg procedure as described above.
27|Non-inferiority will be tested only at the completion of the study. Secondary endpoints will
28|only be tested once, at the completion of the trial or if the decision is made to terminate the
29|trial early. If the study terminates early for superiority, the key secondary endpoints of CV
30|death, MI, stroke and all-cause mortality will be tested at the same significance level as the
31|primary endpoint in the interim analysis using the hierarchical test strategy. Additional
32|efficacy endpoints will be tested at the 2-sided 0.05 level.

34|Censoring
35|4.1.2.1
36|Censoring Scheme
37|Primary Censoring Scheme: in time-to-event analyses in the ITT population, patients will be
38|censored at the earliest of: 1) date of last contact where all elements of the endpoint could be

Statistical Analysis Plan
Study Code D5551C00003(BCB109)
Edition Number 4
February 23rd 2017
21
assessed, and 2) the date of last dose of study medication, and 3) the right censoring date.
Patients who never start the study drug will be censored at randomization.
On-treatment + n days Censoring Scheme (where n=7, 30, and 70): patients will be censored
at the earliest of: 1) date of last contact where all elements of the endpoint could be assessed,
2) the date of last dose of study medication + n days, and 3) the right censoring date. Patients
who never start the study drug will be censored at randomization.
Cut-off Date Censoring Scheme: patients will be censored at the earliest of: 1) date of last
contact where all elements of the endpoint could be assessed, and 2) the primary endpoint cut
off date. The primary endpoint cut off date will be determined by the Executive Committee as
the date when the sites will start bringing patients back for the Trial Termination visit. Patients
without any assessment of the endpoint will be censored at randomization.
Right censoring date is defined as the last known alive date as collected at the trial termination
visit (TTV form) except for deceased patients where it is the adjudicated date of the death.
4.1.2.2
Assumption on Non-informative Censoring
The time to event analysis (Cox regression) relies on the assumption of non-informative
censoring. To examine this assumption, variables that may be related to censoring, for
example, the most frequent major protocol deviation, certain SAEs, will be explored. Rates
per 100 patient-years will be calculated per treatment group and compared between patients
censored early without complete follow-up, and those with complete follow-up.
To assess possible effects of informative censoring on the primary efficacy endpoint,
sensitivity analyses will be done as follows. First, the tipping point analysis will be performed
where in patients who prematurely discontinued the study without having a primary endpoint
event prior to discontinuation, events will be imputed during their missing follow up time (i.e.
time from censoring to trial termination visit) under various scenarios for the hazard rates for
non-completers in each arm. For each scenario, 2000 imputations will be performed and the
results will be combined across 2000 combined datasets (actual events in completers +
imputed events in non-completers) using SAS PROC MIANALYZE. Specifically, log-hazard
ratio estimate of treatment effect will be calculated as an average and its associated variance
will be obtained using Rubin's8 (1987) formula, which combines within-imputation and
between-imputation variances. Hazard ratios, Wald's 95% CIs and Wald's test p-values will
also be calculated. The goal of this analysis is to find scenarios where the primary analysis
results will be "tipped", i.e. the conclusion will change.
4.2
Study Conduct
Major protocol deviations will be identified for all patients who are randomized (see Section
2.2).
